cue: How do you say someone is doing something completely pointless?

es.literal: to throw water into the sea
es.meaning: To do something entirely pointless, adding to what is already abundant.
es.example: Explicarle las reglas otra vez es echar agua al mar: hace lo que quiere de todos modos.
es.exampleTranslation: Explaining the rules to him again is pointless — he does as he likes regardless.
es.regionNote: Wider LatAm currency plausible but unverified — reviewer to extend or trim.

it.literal: to carry water to the sea
it.meaning: To do something entirely pointless, adding to what is already abundant.
it.example: Regalargli un'altra cravatta è come portare acqua al mare: ne ha già un cassetto pieno.
it.exampleTranslation: Giving him another tie is pointless — he already has a drawerful.

bridge.note: Same futile errand, different verb doing the work. Spanish throws the water — echar, a quick disposal — while Italian carries it — portare, which makes the whole thing worse by adding the effort of the journey to the pointlessness of the arrival. Italian also keeps a bench of rival phrases for the same idea, portare vasi a Samo and portare coccodrilli in Egitto among them, where Spanish settles on the sea.

interference.es_to_it: The verb does not cross. 'Gettare acqua al mare' or 'buttare acqua al mare' both read as literal descriptions of throwing water; the idiom takes portare. Note also that Italian may reach for portare vasi a Samo instead, which has no Spanish counterpart at all.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish does not carry the water, it throws it: echar agua al mar. 'Llevar agua al mar' is comprehensible but is not the fixed form.
